The bytes themselves are the wiki source of a Latin Wikisource transcription, and Latin Wikisource contributions are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 — a condition on the contributors' markup rather than on Migne's text under it. The exact bytes are therefore hashed and recorded but not retained here, and only the printed Latin reaches the tracked derivative, stripped of every template, link, heading and column marker the contributors and the encoder added.

edition.notes: The ancient Latin version of Basil's nine Hexaemeron homilies, made by Eustathius at the request of the deaconess Syncletica about 440, and the form in which the work reached the Latin West: Bede's own preface names Basil "quem Eustathius interpres de Graeco fecit esse Latinum" among the three fathers he follows. It is a separate EDITION of Basil's work and not a separate work, and not a second text on one edition. Nine books answering the nine homilies, preceded by Eustathius's dedicatory letter, which is part of the version and not of Basil. The printing is Migne's of 1847; the translation is of the fifth century and its translator died in antiquity, so nothing here is in copyright anywhere.
edition.publication: Patrologia Latina, tomus 53, Paris: J.-P. Migne, 1847, coll. 867-966
edition.title: Metaphrasis Latina Hexaemeri, the Latin version of Eustathius

work.author: Basil of Caesarea
work.description: Basil's nine Lenten homilies on the six days of creation, delivered at Caesarea in 378. A locus is the homily and, where needed, its numbered section. The series expounds Genesis 1:1 to 1:26 and stops there: the ninth homily breaks off before the creation of man, and the work has no extent past that verse. The record exists so that a fragment translated inside a Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers volume can name Basil as its author rather than the volume's editors.
work.title: Homiliae in Hexaemeron
